question: On 24 December 2025, the Italian Armed Forces General Staff announced in a memorandum that, pursuant to Article 1477b(2)(a) of the Italian Military Code, it was removing a member of the armed forces from his position as a trade union1 leader. This decision came nine days after CGARS2 Judgement No 1004 confirmed the legality of the serviceman’s two-month suspension from duty3.

On 15 January, an appeal was lodged before the Regional Administrative Court of Sicily which, among other things, highlighted that the defendant had been automatically removed from his trade union role and that his case had not been individually assessed.

In the light of the provisions outlined by Article 2 TEU and Articles 11, 12, 51 and 52 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and having regard for CJEU case-law, we ask the Commission: 1.

Will it request information from the Italian authorities with a view to ensuring that any restrictions on the freedom of association and expression of armed forces members are necessary and proportionate and do not deter military personnel from exercising their fundamental rights and their right to union membership?

Which Union instruments – including rule of law dialogues and infringement proceedings – would be appropriate for dealing with cases in which restrictions akin to the above run counter to the values espoused by Article 2 TEU and the rights enshrined in the Charter?

These organisations are officially known as APCSMs (Associazione professionale a carattere sindacale tra militari). Council of Administrative Justice for the Sicily Region. These suspensions are reserved for defendants whose serious disciplinary offences make their continued service in the armed forces temporarily impossible.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) 1. The Commission supports social dialogue in line with the provisions of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union recognises the freedom of assembly and association and the right of collective bargaining and action1.

However, the right of association does not fall under the EU’s legislative competence2. The functioning of national social dialogue frameworks falls therefore under the responsibility of each Member State3.

At the same time, the Council Recommendation on strengthening social dialogue in the EU recommends to Member States that they ensure ‘an enabling environment for bipartite and tripartite social dialogue’ in the public and private sectors4. 2.

As regards the case referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission recalls that, according to its Article 51(1), the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law.

Where an alleged violation of fundamental rights derives from a national legal measure, it is primarily the responsibility of national courts to safeguard the rights of individuals. The Commission cannot take over a decision-making role in place of national authorities nor review decisions they have made in individual cases.
1 Article 12 and 28 of the Charter of fundamental Rights of the European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:12012P/TXT&from=EN. 2 Article 153(5) TFEU. 3 The freedom of association and the right for of social partners to organise themselves is enshrined in the

Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention of the International Labour Organisation (ILO), 1948 (No. 87), which all Member States have ratified. The standard supervisory system of the ILO may assess compliance by a Member State with the international labour standards. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/AUTO/?uri=consil:ST_10542_2023_INIT, based on a proposal from the Commission - COM(2023) 38 final, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52023DC0038.
